Preliminary results · working draft · Stata 16 design

Paid Family Leave, Mothers' Labour Supply and Parents' Mental Health

Staggered adoption of state paid family and medical leave, 2004–2024, estimated with Callaway–Sant'Anna group-time effects. Part I: labour supply and fertility on IPUMS-CPS ASEC repeated cross sections, 1990–2025 (nine cohorts, 1.2 million women aged 18–44). Part II: exposure at birth and parents' mental health one to five years later in the NSCH, 2016–2024.

Repository branch claude/female-labor-participation-research-6l2899, results in docs/results.md · September 2026

Produced by python/02_csdid.py and summarised by 04_summarise.py; the Stata mirror is stata/02_csdid.do; subgroups by python/05_heterogeneity.sh and stata/05_heterogeneity.do.

1Question

Nine states and the District of Columbia now pay wage replacement to parents of newborns and to workers caring for family members, with programmes that differ in duration (4 to 20 weeks), replacement rates (50 to 95 percent) and job protection. Does paid leave raise mothers' labour force attachment, on which margin, for whom, and do the second-generation programmes have larger effects than California's? The evidence rests mostly on California and New Jersey and disagrees: employment continuity around births in the short run, lower employment and earnings for first-time mothers six to ten years later. A design that uses every cohort with one estimator, keeps cohorts separate, and measures the response month by month is the contribution.

2Identification

Treatment is the availability of benefits in the mother's state, timed to the month benefits became payable. With staggered adoption and dynamic effects, two-way fixed effects use already-treated states as controls for later cohorts and are biased. We estimate group-time average treatment effects

ATT(g, t) = E[Yt − Yg−1 | G = g] − E[Yt − Yg−1 | C]

with C the never-treated states (main) or the not-yet-treated states (robustness), aggregated to event time, cohort and calendar time with cohort-size weights. Estimation is doubly robust (csdid, method(drimp)) with age, marital status, race, ethnicity and education, on CPS repeated cross sections, with a wild bootstrap clustered by state. Because state shocks hit all women, the same event studies for childless women are the placebo and the triple difference (mothers of under-6s minus childless women) is the fallback specification.

4Data

IPUMS-CPS ASEC 1990–2025Extract cps_00090 (all persons; 6.35 million records), restricted to women 18–44: 1,216,812 person-years, reference years 1989–2024. Mothers and the age of the youngest own child come from the IPUMS pointers (NCHILD, YNGCH, NCHLT5). Outcomes: worked last year (WORKLY), weeks, usual hours last year, full time, plus March labour-force status.
CohortsFirst reference year with at least six months of benefits: CA 2004, NJ 2009, RI 2014, NY 2018, WA and DC 2020, MA 2021, CT 2022, OR 2023, CO 2024. DE, MN and MD adopt after the window and are never-treated controls. About 10,500 mothers of under-6s per year; 816,000 person-years in never-treated states.
Buildpython/01_build_ipums_asec.py and stata/01_build_cps_asec.do produce the same file; every IPUMS code used was checked against the extract.

8Heterogeneous effects

The headline specification re-estimated within subgroups. Income is measured two ways that are not outcomes: education, which fixes earnings potential and hence where a mother sits relative to each programme's benefit cap, and other family income (family income minus her own labour income) in within-year terciles.

  • Income, education, marital status: no heterogeneity. Every subgroup sits between 0 and +4 points with standard errors of 2 to 3 points and flat pre-trends; no pair differs by more than one standard error.
  • Race and ethnicity: the whole effect is white non-Hispanic mothers. +5.4 points and +2.2 hours, growing with exposure (+3 in year 0, +5 to +9 in years 5 to 10) and concentrated in California (+7.5, s.e. 2.7) and New Jersey (+4.7, s.e. 4.4); zero for Black, Hispanic and other mothers. The white-minus-Hispanic gap is 6 points (s.e. 3.1).
  • Births show no heterogeneity: every subgroup is within one point of zero.

Two checks on the white-mother effect

  • Placebo passes. Childless white women in California and New Jersey show no change, so the white-mother effect is not a white-population trend. The implied triple difference for white mothers is +4.8 points.
  • Eligibility does not explain it. Prior-year work rates are 0.73 for white and 0.72 for Black mothers, so take-up cannot produce the white-Black gap; and among linked mothers the effect sits with prior non-workers (+4.5, s.e. 3.2), not prior workers (−2.4, s.e. 2.0), the opposite of a take-up mechanism.
  • Open question: migration. The linked sample is address-stayers, and in it the white-mother effect is absent (+1.4, s.e. 3.6; California +0.1). The gap to the full-sample +5.4 is within noise, but a composition effect from recent movers into CA and NJ is open. The direct test is the ACS, which records state of residence one year earlier.

9Reading

  • A precise null at the extensive margin. With nine cohorts and 35 years the design rules out employment effects above about 5 points for mothers of pre-schoolers, and the placebo and pre-trends behave. This contrasts with large short-run effects reported for California from birth-timed samples and is consistent with PFML acting on leave-taking and job continuity around births rather than on the stock of employed mothers.
  • A late rise driven by California and New Jersey. Coefficients drift to +3 to +4 points and +1 to +1.6 hours in years seven to ten. Only the first two cohorts identify those horizons, so this is a two-state pattern, and it runs against the negative long-run findings for first-time mothers in California.
  • Generation comparison is underpowered. First-generation programmes (CA, NJ, RI) have positive point estimates of 2 to 4 points; the more generous 2018–2024 programmes average about zero with one to six post-years and wide intervals.
  • Caveats. Calendar-year timing assigns a whole year to cohorts whose benefits started mid-year (a first-full-year cohort variable is in the file); policy dates are from memory and must be verified; standard errors are a state block bootstrap and should be compared with csdid's wild cluster bootstrap in Stata.

10Part II: paid leave at birth and parents' mental health (NSCH)

Because the labour-supply and fertility results are precise nulls, the second part of the project asks whether paid leave at a child's birth leaves a mark on the parent's mental health one to five years later. Wells et al. (2026, AJE) find lower postpartum depressive symptoms two to six months after birth in PRAMS; the National Survey of Children's Health (2016–2024, 386,083 sampled children) asks the responding parent's own mental and physical health for a child of any age, so exposure can be defined at the birth and the parent observed years afterwards, with fathers included and the 2018–2024 programmes covered. The time index is the child's birth year and the cohort is the state's first birth year with at least six months of benefits; controls are births in the same year in never-treated states. Design: docs/nsch_design.md; results: docs/nsch_results.md.

Suggestive, not settled. For a real effect: flat pre-trends, zero calendar-time placebos, a stronger estimate where exposure is measured accurately, the gradient towards lower-income and less-educated mothers, and fathers moving the same way. Against: the mother's physical health moves as much as her mental health, the fair/poor margin (closest to depressive symptoms) does not move, and half the magnitude comes from New York. With seven treated clusters the block-bootstrap standard errors are rough; the Stata version (stata/21_csdid_nsch.do, drimp with survey-year and age covariates, wild cluster bootstrap) is the inference to report.

11Stata pipeline

00_master.doPaths, logging, package list, runs everything; falls back to the preliminary demo if the IPUMS extract is absent.
01_build_cps.doIPUMS-CPS basic monthly 2000–2024 to the estimation file: outcomes, family structure, cohort variables at monthly and yearly precision, state-cell panels.
02_csdid.doMain estimates: csdid with never-treated controls, drimp, covariates, wild cluster bootstrap; estat simple / group / calendar / event / pretrend; yearly and monthly cohorts; cohort-generation heterogeneity.
03_robustness.doNot-yet-treated controls, triple difference, alternative cohort timing, childless placebo, Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess, Sun–Abraham, de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille, HonestDiD sensitivity, TWFE for reference.
04_tables.doesttab tables for the paper.
20_build_nsch.do · 21_csdid_nsch.doNSCH build and the mental-health estimates: mothers 0–5 by outcome, age bands, fathers, calendar-time placebo, robustness (base g−2, not-yet, year-minus-age, no 2020–21, surveys 2019+, no New York), heterogeneity.

The do-files are untested: the build environment has no Stata. Two known checks on first run are listed in stata/README.md.

12Next steps

  • Run 00_master.do in Stata 16 on the same extract for covariate-adjusted (drimp) estimates, the wild cluster bootstrap, and the robustness set (not-yet-treated, triple difference, Sun–Abraham, BJS, HonestDiD).
  • Mothers of infants and the March survey-week outcomes, which date labour supply after the leave rather than the calendar year it started.
  • Verify every date in the policy panel and add programme parameters (weeks, replacement rate, job protection) as moderators.
  • Reconcile the late CA/NJ rise with the birth-timed literature; add fathers as a second placebo.
  • NSCH: run the Stata version for wild-bootstrap inference; add the 2025 file when released (post-periods for Connecticut, Oregon, Colorado); use the reported birth month for exact exposure; randomisation inference over placebo cohorts; check the physical-health finding externally (PRAMS or ACS general health).
